status: Exact shared row fields and kind enums; NOT runtime-admitted. Empty registry names deliberately represent unsupported bindings.
limits: No new per-law month.ts/index.ts claims. Existing stamp batch1302 remains separate first-version source.
No numeric outcome default, drawn level, pooled study coefficient or invented unit cost.
Existing map link references are inventory, not endorsement or fresh activation; about-zero and units require exact study review.
Real government jurisdiction/preemption/operative dates and actual saved beneficiaries are required.
Repeal changes prospective legal obligations/service according to operative terms; it does not undo paid transfers, completed education or past case outcomes.
All empty selector/action/record names must fail admission; this payload must not activate as-is.
No extra lag follows the actual saved activity; zero direct-row lag is processing at that activity date, not an estimated study lag. Onward study lags are unadmitted.
Capacity and exposure may enter amount expressions only with registered actual-record keys; none were invented.
Onward source records are unchanged inventory, not numerical endorsement, pooling or new activation.

sourceRecord.anchor: School finance reforms raised spending and achievement in low-income districts (to confirm)
why: An equalization act changes the allocation formula or appropriation for qualifying districts.
The formula redirects state aid because district taxable wealth otherwise limits locally raised resources.
The treasury can pay that aid only from an actual revenue appropriation or recorded borrowing.
The district receives resources only when the authorized transfer is made.
Bedrock is the legal allocation rule and treasury-to-district receipt; a binary act alone is not a dollar receipt.

strongerWhen: Low-property-wealth districts receive a larger formula increase.
weakerWhen: A district was already above the new funding guarantee.
absentWhen: No operative funding provision, appropriation or qualifying district is recorded.

sourceRecord.reverseOnRepeal: Repeal changes future allocation authority. It does not remove money already received by a district or supplies already bought. The existing aggregate law-answer reversal must not rewrite budget history.
sourceRecord.who: Qualifying districts and their enrolled pupils; residents funding the state budget bear the financing trade-off.
sourceRecord.lagWhy: The existing12-month lag stands for an allocation/budget cycle; it is not a verified causal delay. Team9 must provide timing and per-pupil funding contrast from the cited reform study.

sourceRecord.anchor: School finance reforms raise spending in low-income districts at once, and achievement there rises over the following years; the implied effect of resources is large (size to confirm).
why: A qualifying school can change instructional inputs after receiving additional funding.
The school can hire or retain staff and obtain instructional resources only when those resources are available.
The changed inputs affect a pupil only if their recorded school and instruction expose them to the change.
Sustained instructional exposure can change the skills measured by a later math assessment.
Bedrock is actual instruction received and assessment performance; no pupil score is produced by a statewide formula here.

strongerWhen: A low-income district begins with scarce instructional resources and the money buys relevant inputs.
weakerWhen: Starting spending is already high or the measured treatment is a smaller funding increase.
absentWhen: The pupil is not enrolled in an affected school or no funded input changes.

sourceRecord.reverseOnRepeal: Repeal can end future input funding; it does not subtract a pupil learned skill or erase an earlier assessment. A future assessment needs newly observed conditions, not an immediate negative score.
sourceRecord.who: Pupils actually exposed in qualifying districts; statewide proficiency needs enrollment-weighted cohort evidence.
sourceRecord.lagWhy: The existing36-month lag approximates resource delivery and several school years of exposure. The cited study horizon and statewide proficiency conversion remain unverified.

sourceRecord.anchor: 10% more per student every year raises completed schooling 0.31 years, far more for low-income children; statewide about +2% on the rate once cohorts pass through (size to confirm).
why: Additional district resources can change staffing and support available to enrolled pupils.
A pupil can persist when their own attendance, support and academic circumstances permit it.
Persistence creates additional completed school work and progress toward recorded requirements.
A diploma follows completion of those actual requirements.
Bedrock is an individual completed schooling record, not a random graduation-rate assignment.

strongerWhen: Resource-constrained, low-income pupils receive sustained exposure before completion.
weakerWhen: Funding arrives late in the cohort schooling or support does not reach the pupil.
absentWhen: The pupil has already graduated or attends an unaffected school.

sourceRecord.reverseOnRepeal: Repeal affects future support for still-enrolled cohorts. A completed diploma remains a historical fact and cannot be undone by a law-answer reversal.
sourceRecord.who: Exposed school-age cohorts, particularly the low-income districts studied; not all adult residents.
sourceRecord.lagWhy: The existing60-month lag represents progression toward completion. Actual ages, exposure years and completion dates must replace a generic five-year switch.

sourceRecord.anchor: Statewide voucher users lost ground in math at first (Louisiana, Indiana, Ohio), fading after a few years; few students use them, so the state moves little.
sourceRecord.source: Abdulkadiroglu, Pathak and Walters 2018; Waddington and Berends 2018 (to confirm)
why: A funded award can give an eligible household another school choice.
The household can use it only if an eligible school has a place and the remaining charge/transport is feasible.
Enrollment changes the instruction the pupil actually receives.
That instruction may improve or worsen the skills measured by later math assessments.
Bedrock is a family decision, paid award and school enrollment; private status alone does not imply higher quality.

strongerWhen: The voucher causes an actual school change with materially different instruction.
weakerWhen: The award subsidizes an enrollment that would happen anyway.
absentWhen: No award, school place, eligibility or recorded enrollment change exists.

sourceRecord.reverseOnRepeal: Repeal stops prospective award authority. It does not erase the award already paid or the pupil prior instruction. A subsequent return to another school needs a household decision and enrollment record.
sourceRecord.who: Voucher-using pupils and their households, with school/provider-specific effects; nonparticipants cannot be assigned the recipient estimate.
sourceRecord.lagWhy: The existing12-month lag represents a school year before assessment. Verify the cited voucher study follow-up and treatment group; a state-wide diluted coefficient is not the trial estimate.

sourceRecord.anchor: D.C. voucher users graduated more (about +12 points for users); few students use them.
why: A voucher award can make a chosen private-school enrollment feasible.
The household must choose that school and the school must accept the pupil.
The resulting school experience can alter continued attendance and progress.
Graduation occurs only when the pupil completes the applicable requirements.
Bedrock is a funded choice and completed schooling, not a voucher law assigning a diploma.

strongerWhen: A participating pupil attends a school whose completion support differs from the counterfactual school.
weakerWhen: Few eligible pupils participate or the award does not change their school.
absentWhen: The pupil is not a participant or already completed school before exposure.

sourceRecord.reverseOnRepeal: Repeal can remove funding for future enrollment choices. Previously completed schooling remains; a remaining pupil graduation consequence depends on their later school path.
sourceRecord.who: Actual voucher participants in the study cohorts; statewide graduation requires measured participation and cohort shares.
sourceRecord.lagWhy: The existing48-month lag approximates later graduation, but the pupil grade and cited follow-up define when completion could actually change.

sourceRecord.anchor: 10% higher teacher pay cuts dropouts 3 to 4%; a state salary floor is assumed to raise average teacher pay about 5%
sourceRecord.source: Loeb and Page 2000, Review of Economics and Statistics 82(3)
why: An operative salary floor requires a covered public employer to raise under-floor teacher compensation.
The employer changes saved pay terms and pays that amount in actual pay periods.
Higher pay may change retention or recruitment only through a teacher or applicant employment decision.
The changed staffing may alter instruction for the pupils assigned to those teachers.
Bedrock for the direct effect is a legal pay requirement; the graduation continuation needs actual employment, instruction and completion records.

strongerWhen: The floor binds many underpaid covered teachers and resources permit staffing responses.
weakerWhen: Existing salary is already above the floor or the pay rise is small.
absentWhen: A private teacher is outside coverage, the first applicable school year has not begun, or no staffing/instruction change reaches the pupil.

sourceRecord.reverseOnRepeal: Repeal removes the future legal floor. It does not cut saved teacher pay or revoke a diploma; any staffing response must follow actual later employment terms and decisions.
sourceRecord.who: Under-floor covered public-school teachers first; only pupils taught by affected staffing can receive an indirect educational consequence.
sourceRecord.lagWhy: The existing24-month graduation lag is a model approximation. Salary changes begin with the legally operative school year/pay period; staffing and cohort completion need their own dated exposure.

sourceRecord.anchor: D.C. universal pre-K: +10 points in mothers' participation (about +15% on its base); Quebec child care about +7%
why: A funded preschool place can provide care during specific hours.
The parent benefits only when the child is enrolled and the schedule covers their care constraint.
That coverage can make a particular job schedule feasible.
The parent still needs an available job offer and must choose it given pay, travel and family circumstances.
Bedrock is actual child care and a parent hiring decision, not a participation multiplier choosing employment.

strongerWhen: The parent had binding care costs/schedule constraints and an accessible job.
weakerWhen: The household already had equivalent care or only part-day care is provided.
absentWhen: No preschool place, child enrollment, usable schedule or feasible job exists.

sourceRecord.reverseOnRepeal: Repeal may end a future funded care place after its lawful phase-out. It does not automatically dismiss an employed mother; she reassesses care and work from actual records.
sourceRecord.who: Parents of eligible enrolled young children whose care constraint changes; the cited maternal estimate is not all women or every household.
sourceRecord.lagWhy: The existing12-month lag represents enrollment and labor response. Verify the D.C./Quebec study time window and whether the effect is percentage points or a relative participation change.

sourceRecord.anchor: Boston's universal preschool: +6 points on-time graduation for children who enrolled; with about 70% enrolled, about +5% of a state's rate, 14 years after the first four-year-olds. Tennessee's program did worse; quality decides where in the range a world lands.
sourceRecord.source: Gray-Lobe, Pathak and Walters 2023; Vanderbilt TN-VPK
why: A preschool program offers a place with particular instructional quality.
A child obtains the educational exposure only through actual enrollment and attendance.
The instruction and later school context can alter skills and persistence.
The exposed cohort reaches the age and requirements for high-school completion years later.
Bedrock is child attendance followed by completed schooling; quality differences explain why program studies need separate conditions.

strongerWhen: The funded program provides the quality and population exposure of the favorable study.
weakerWhen: Program quality, follow-on schooling or participant share differs from that study.
absentWhen: The child does not attend or is not yet old enough for the measured completion outcome.

sourceRecord.reverseOnRepeal: Repeal ends future offered places. It cannot delete an earlier child exposure or a completed diploma; the already exposed cohort may retain long-term effects.
sourceRecord.who: Actual enrolled preschool cohorts as they reach high-school age; not present-day adults or all children in the state.
sourceRecord.lagWhy: The existing168-month lag follows four-year-olds toward high-school graduation. It is fourteen years, so a24-month audit must report not-yet-due rather than missing firing.

That exposure changes learning experiences only for the attending child.
Later school instruction can reinforce or offset that experience.
A later math assessment records the skills then acquired.
Bedrock is actual instruction and assessment; adverse Tennessee and null test findings cannot become a universal positive score.

strongerWhen: Program and subsequent schooling resemble the measured comparison.
weakerWhen: Quality or later-school context differs from the evaluated program.
absentWhen: There is no enrolled exposure or no assessment at the relevant follow-up.

sourceRecord.reverseOnRepeal: Repeal affects future attendance opportunities. It does not erase an assessment or reverse learned skills; subsequent instruction needs its own path.
sourceRecord.who: Enrolled preschool pupils at the study follow-up ages and programs; statewide dilution remains a separate unverified conversion.
sourceRecord.lagWhy: The existing60-month lag represents later elementary assessment. Verify the exact grade/follow-up and quality-specific sign before numeric activation.
